intros: A closer look at the era of the American Civil War.
The Civil War left its mark on almost every object of its time.
Some pieces of the past still speak clearly across 160 years.
Here is a piece of the Civil War era worth a second look.
Museums keep these objects so the stories behind them are not forgotten.
contexts: The American Civil War was fought from 1861 to 1865.
The war began on April 12, 1861, when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina.
Abraham Lincoln was sworn in as the 16th President of the United States on March 4, 1861.
Eleven Southern states left the Union and formed the Confederate States of America, with Jefferson Davis as its president.
The First Battle of Bull Run, fought on July 21, 1861, in Virginia, showed both sides that the war would not be short.
On March 9, 1862, the ironclads USS Monitor and CSS Virginia fought to a draw at Hampton Roads, Virginia.
The Battle of Antietam, fought in Maryland on September 17, 1862, is often called the bloodiest single day in American military history.
President Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863.
Harriet Tubman helped lead the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina in June 1863, which freed hundreds of enslaved people.
The Battle of Gettysburg was fought from July 1 to 3, 1863, in Pennsylvania.
Confederate forces at Vicksburg, Mississippi, surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant on July 4, 1863.
President Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a national cemetery for Union soldiers.
Roughly 180,000 Black men served in the Union Army as United States Colored Troops.
Frederick Douglass, a formerly enslaved abolitionist, urged Black men to enlist in the Union Army.
Photographers such as Mathew Brady and Alexander Gardner brought the realities of the war to the public through their pictures.
Clara Barton cared for wounded soldiers during the war and founded the American Red Cross in 1881.
General William T. Sherman's forces captured Atlanta, Georgia, in September 1864.
General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on April 9, 1865.
President Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C., on April 14, 1865, and died the next morning.
The Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery in the United States, was ratified in December 1865.
Historians estimate that between 620,000 and 750,000 soldiers died in the Civil War.
